title: Windows Time Offset and Synchronization Error
exclusions: Evaluates the newest valid Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows `Script:TimesyncStatus` sample per covered host and returns it when absolute `Phase_Offset` is strictly greater than the locally selected 120-second limit or the parsed `Last_Sync_Error` code is nonzero. It does not prove UTC accuracy, measure every interval, validate the configured peer or domain hierarchy, detect a host that never reports, distinguish a malicious clock change, repair time, or guarantee Kerberos/log integrity. `Phase_Offset` is interpreted as signed seconds only after installed-add-on and `w32tm /query /status /verbose` parity testing. Exactly 120 seconds does not breach. The 120-second threshold and 15-minute freshness window are local early-warning choices, not Microsoft, Kerberos, NTP, or Splunk defaults; the documented Kerberos five-minute policy is context, not this alert threshold. Documentation-only review does not establish production operation or compliance.
evidence: Retain covered-host/time-role inventory; effective W32Time Group Policy and runtime configuration; installed Splunk Add-on version; enabled TimeSyncStatus/TimeSyncConfiguration input stanzas; raw `Script:TimesyncStatus` samples; same-time `w32tm /query /source`, `/configuration`, `/peers`, and `/status /verbose` output; `windows_time_offset_or_sync_error` saved-search definition, ACL, schedule, dispatch history, and rows; source/field-health searches; threshold policy; dashboard/alert revisions; bounded maintenance lookup; incident dispositions; and dated positive, negative, exact-120-second, signed-offset, unit, stale, malformed, duplicate, locale/version, recovery, and suppression tests. Each finding preserves sample/event and index time, host/dest, phase offset raw and normalized seconds, last-sync-error raw/code, source, stratum, reference ID, last successful sync time, time since last good sync, poll interval, role, source type, input/add-on version, and exception decision. This review generated no live artefacts.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated index, add current `sourcetype=Script:TimesyncStatus` samples for `host=time-lab-01` with `Phase_Offset=-120.001s` and `Last_Sync_Error=0 (The command completed successfully.)`, and `host=time-lab-02` with `Phase_Offset=0.010s` and `Last_Sync_Error=5 (Access is denied.)`; expect exactly two rows with reasons `offset_over_120_seconds` and `last_sync_error`. Verify the first normalizes to absolute `offset_seconds=120.001` and the second to `last_sync_error_code=5`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Add current valid samples with `Phase_Offset=120.000s` and error code 0, `Phase_Offset=-119.999s` and code 0, plus an older breach followed by a newest healthy sample for the same host; expect zero rows because the boundary is strict and only the newest valid sample is evaluated. Also expect zero primary rows for a sample older than 15 minutes or one with an unparseable/missing phase offset or error code; those malformed/stale conditions must appear in separate source-health output.

dataSources: Primary source: the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742) scripted status input with `sourcetype=Script:TimesyncStatus`, enabled on each governed Windows host and routed to the deployment-selected index. Splunk documents this source type as Windows time synchronization status and maps it to Performance; the add-on also supplies `Script:TimesyncConfiguration` for configuration context. Required, version-qualified status fields are `Phase_Offset`, `Last_Sync_Error`, `Source`, `Stratum`, `ReferenceId`, `Last_Successful_Sync_Time`, `Poll_Interval`, `Time_since_Last_Good_Sync_Time`, `Server_Role`, `dest`, and raw/input metadata. Compare their exact names, locale representation, and units with `w32tm /query /status /verbose` on every supported Windows/add-on combination.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) supplies the TimeSyncStatus/TimeSyncConfiguration scripted inputs, parsing, and Performance mapping. A deployment-owned monitoring app should hold inventory, source/field health, saved search, threshold and exception lookups, fixtures, dashboard, and runbook.
spl:
index=windows sourcetype="Script:TimesyncStatus" earliest=-15m@m latest=@m
| eval offset_seconds=abs(tonumber(replace(trim(Phase_Offset),"(?i)s$",""))), last_sync_error_code=tonumber(replace(trim(Last_Sync_Error),"^([0-9]+).*$","\\1")), sample_host=coalesce(dest,host)
| where len(sample_host)>0 AND isnotnull(offset_seconds) AND isnotnull(last_sync_error_code)
| sort 0 sample_host - _time - _indextime
| dedup sample_host
| where offset_seconds>120 OR last_sync_error_code!=0
| eval reason=case(offset_seconds>120 AND last_sync_error_code!=0,"offset_and_last_sync_error",offset_seconds>120,"offset_over_120_seconds",true(),"last_sync_error"), use_case="UC-1.2.109"
| table _time _indextime sample_host host dest reason offset_seconds Phase_Offset last_sync_error_code Last_Sync_Error Source Stratum ReferenceId Last_Successful_Sync_Time Time_since_Last_Good_Sync_Time Poll_Interval Server_Role sourcetype use_case
| sort 0 - offset_seconds sample_host
description: Selects the newest parseable Windows Time status sample for each host in a 15-minute lookback and returns one row when its absolute phase offset exceeds 120 seconds or its last synchronization error code is nonzero. The row reports current sampled status and context; event count is not drift, and stale or malformed hosts are handled by a separate health search.
value: Large or failed clock synchronization can disrupt domain authentication, certificate and token checks, event ordering, backup/database coordination, and incident timelines before a machine becomes obviously unreachable. A normalized host-level result points operators to the observed source, role, offset, and last error while preserving enough margin below the commonly documented five-minute Kerberos tolerance for controlled investigation.
implementation: Enable and qualify the add-on's TimeSyncStatus and TimeSyncConfiguration scripted inputs on covered Windows hosts, route them to the local `windows` index, and compare parsed fields with same-time `w32tm` status/configuration. Save the SPL as `windows_time_offset_or_sync_error`, schedule it every five minutes, and alert on any result using the local >120-second or nonzero-error policy. Operate host freshness, parser/unit, input-error, and time-hierarchy checks separately; recover only through the Windows/AD time-service runbook.
visualization: Dashboard `Windows — Time Synchronization`: put missing/stale/malformed hosts and input failures first; chart signed and absolute phase offset in seconds with labeled ±120-second local alert lines and the separately labeled effective Kerberos tolerance; show last error, source, stratum, reference ID, last good sync age, poll interval, server role, forest/domain/site, virtualization provider, owner, and exception. Separate forest-root PDC, other DCs, members, workgroup hosts, and high-accuracy workloads. Drill down to raw status/configuration samples, same-time `w32tm` outputs, System Time-Service events, GPO/runtime source, hypervisor events, NTP reachability, and incident. Never plot missing offset as zero or convert error silence into healthy.
schema: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows Script:TimesyncStatus field contract
dataModelAcceleration: Splunk documents `Script:TimesyncStatus` as Performance-mapped, but the primary rule depends on add-on-specific `Phase_Offset`, `Last_Sync_Error`, source, reference, role, and last-good-sync fields plus newest-sample semantics. Validate installed tags and normalized fields before optional acceleration. A generic Performance `tstats` aggregate cannot replace signed offset units, error parsing, freshness, or raw-status evidence; any summary must pass host-by-host parity.

knownFalsePositives:
A result is a real parsed status sample crossing local policy or carrying a nonzero last-sync error; business impact and authorization still require context.

1. **Boot, resume, snapshot restore, or live migration** — A VM or physical host can report a temporary phase offset or stale last error while W32Time reacquires its source. Correlate boot/resume/migration time, hypervisor time-provider events, next three samples, and application health. Repeated recurrence is a configuration problem.

2. **Forest-root PDC or authoritative source maintenance** — Planned upstream clock, network, DNS, firewall, PDC-role, or hardware-reference work can produce errors across many descendants. Confirm exact maintenance scope, hierarchy, approved sources, start/expiry, and post-change convergence; do not suppress all domain members indefinitely.

3. **Group Policy or time-source transition** — A reviewed change from domain hierarchy to manual peers, or a PDC role transfer, can briefly change source and offset. Compare `Script:TimesyncConfiguration`, effective GPO/runtime settings, role holder, peer status, and change ticket.

4. **Windows Time clock correction** — W32Time can step or slew after a bad sample, and the newest sample may capture correction in progress. Verify `w32tm /query /status /verbose`, subsequent offset trend, System events 35/37 and fault events, and whether the workload tolerates the correction.

5. **High network asymmetry or distant NTP source** — Phase/stripchart measurements can be noisy when path delay is asymmetric. Compare round-trip delay with `w32tm /stripchart /rdtsc`, source geography, packet loss, several samples, and a closer approved source. Do not raise a global threshold to hide one path.

6. **Hypervisor integration provider conflict** — Guest W32Time and VM integration time synchronization can compete or legitimately change source. Confirm platform support policy, PDC special handling, host/guest provider state, migration/snapshot history, and ownership before changing either provider.

7. **Add-on upgrade, OS locale, or parser drift** — A release can alter status text or extraction so seconds, commas, signs, or error text parse incorrectly. Compare raw event, installed add-on/default transforms, `w32tm` output, and parser tests. Treat malformed data as source health, never as an offset.

8. **Approved time-correction exercise** — A controlled lab or resilience test may intentionally create a bounded offset/error. Require exact host, exercise ID, owner, approver, start, exclusive expiry, expected maximum, rollback, and successful resynchronization evidence.

**Safe suppression:** apply `lookup windows_time_status_exceptions.csv` after base detection using exact `sample_host,reason`, integer inclusive `valid_from_epoch`, exclusive `valid_until_epoch`, owner, approver, ticket, expected source, and maximum approved offset. Reject wildcards, domain-wide/open-ended rows, missing bounds, and suppression of stale/malformed/source-health results. Preserve base status, lookup revision, and delivery decision.
mitreAttack: N/A (operational Windows clock synchronization monitoring; no adversary behavior or intent is asserted)
detectionType: Newest-sample absolute time offset or synchronization error
hardware: Windows Server and Windows client systems running W32Time and a qualified Splunk Add-on TimeSyncStatus scripted input. Domain members, domain controllers, forest-root PDC emulators, standalone hosts, virtual machines, and high-accuracy workloads require role-specific source and threshold policy; appliances and non-Windows NTP clients require separate collectors.
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against primary Microsoft W32Time tools, hierarchy, technical reference, authoritative-source, no-time-data, and Kerberos tolerance documentation plus Splunk Microsoft Windows add-on TimeSyncStatus source-type/configuration/troubleshooting documentation; input, fields, units, SPL, fixtures, source health, thresholds, alerting, dashboard, scale, and response were specified but not executed or Windows Time/AD/Splunk-SME signed

cost.search_load_notes: At a five-minute cadence, each host contributes about 288 compact status samples per day. The search scans 15 minutes, parses two fields, sorts, and keeps one row per host. Fleet size and scripted-input process overhead, rather than SPL complexity, dominate cost.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites, roles, and units

Assign Windows Time/AD, endpoint/server, virtualization, network/NTP, application, Splunk data/content, and incident owners. Inventory every covered host with stable identity, domain/forest/site, OS/add-on version, physical/virtual platform, W32Time role, expected synchronization mode/source, forest-root PDC status, accuracy objective, application tolerance, owner, onboarding, and retirement time. Separate high-accuracy workloads from ordinary AD authentication requirements.

Microsoft states W32Time is essential to Kerberos and AD DS operations, but not every workload has the same accuracy target. The default/recommended Kerberos maximum clock tolerance is five minutes; this UC uses a local early-warning threshold of absolute phase offset strictly greater than 120 seconds. Exactly 120.000 seconds is healthy for this rule. Select a lower or higher local threshold only from effective Kerberos policy, token/certificate/database/application tolerances, source quality, correction behavior, and response lead time. Never present 120 seconds as a Windows or Splunk default.

The rule interprets `Phase_Offset` as signed seconds because it is derived from `w32tm /query /status /verbose` in the add-on's TimeSyncStatus input. Before deployment, verify the installed script and transforms, raw status output, decimal separator, suffix, sign, and field value. If that parity fails, stop: do not multiply or divide by 1,000 by guesswork.

## Step 1 — Validate the Windows time hierarchy

Document the intended domain hierarchy. Microsoft describes domain clients/member servers selecting authenticating domain controllers, domain controllers following the hierarchy, and the forest-root PDC emulator occupying the top domain position unless another reliable source is configured. Microsoft highly recommends a hardware source for the authoritative server; internet NTP is unauthenticated. Standalone systems and specialized accurate-time designs can differ.

On each policy class, collect read-only baseline commands:

```text
w32tm /query /source
w32tm /query /configuration /verbose
w32tm /query /peers /verbose
w32tm /query /status /verbose
```

Record exact command time, exit status, source, stratum, reference ID, last successful sync, last sync error, phase offset, poll interval, role, runtime setting source, and effective Group Policy. For troubleshooting only, `w32tm /stripchart /computer:<approved-source> /samples:5 /rdtsc` supplies round-trip delay and NTP offset in seconds; it measures the relationship between the querying host and named server and is not interchangeable with the add-on status sample.

Confirm forest-root PDC role transfers update time-source policy. Verify virtualized PDC/provider design with the hypervisor owner. Avoid a loop, local CMOS clock fallback presented as authoritative, or every domain member manually pinned to internet peers contrary to the approved hierarchy.

## Step 2 — Enable and qualify Splunk add-on inputs

Install Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742) on the Universal Forwarder/Windows Splunk instance and required parsing/search tiers according to the supported distributed deployment. Copy the TimeSyncStatus and TimeSyncConfiguration stanzas from the installed `default/inputs.conf` into `local/inputs.conf`, set `disabled=0`, select `index=windows` as the local deployment choice, and retain the vendor-owned script/source/sourcetype values. Do not edit `default` or invent a generic script path from another release.

Splunk documents `Script:TimesyncStatus` for synchronization status and `Script:TimesyncConfiguration` for configuration. Its troubleshooting page states that “service has not been started” output requires investigation of the Windows Time service. Test service startup policy by role; do not blindly force Automatic on systems where Microsoft/organizational policy intentionally uses trigger start.

Use a five-minute interval only after checking the installed default stanza and testing process/runtime load. If changing cadence, version the input, SPL freshness, source-health tolerance, dashboard, and tests together. Splunk Cloud executes this scripted input on customer-managed Windows forwarders, not in the managed search tier.

Verify effective configuration with the platform's supported configuration inspection and deployment tooling. Confirm input enabled once, target index exists, forwarder role can write, search role can read, no duplicate app/stanza, script signature/path intact, W32Time query identity sufficient, output line breaking correct, and host/dest stable. Measure process duration, output bytes, CPU, and indexing delay at scale.

## Step 3 — Prove field and unit extraction

For every supported Windows locale, OS build, add-on release, and W32Time role, capture one raw `Script:TimesyncStatus` event and same-time `w32tm /query /status /verbose`. Verify `Phase_Offset`, `Last_Sync_Error`, `Source`, `Stratum`, `ReferenceId`, `Last_Successful_Sync_Time`, `Time_since_Last_Good_Sync_Time`, `Poll_Interval`, `Server_Role`, `dest`, host, event time, and index time.

Create parser fixtures for `0.001s`, `-0.001s`, `120.000s`, `-120.001s`, comma-decimal locale output if supported, missing suffix, scientific notation if emitted, blank phase, and command error text. The production rule accepts only the qualified decimal-plus-optional-terminal-`s` representation after trim. If locale emits a comma, deploy a tested locale-specific extraction or normalize in the collector; do not globally replace commas that may have other meaning.

`Last_Sync_Error` is accepted only when it starts with a decimal code followed by optional text. Code zero represents no last error in qualified output; nonzero returns a result. A current code zero does not prove uninterrupted synchronization. A stale last-success time with code zero belongs in a companion health rule.

## Step 4 — Establish inventory-backed source health

Run a separate `windows_time_status_source_health` search that compares covered hosts to latest status/configuration sample. Report no sample within two expected intervals plus measured p99 delay, script command failure, unparseable phase/error, missing mandatory fields, unknown/duplicate host identity, future event, excessive event/index skew, unexpected source type/index, status/configuration disagreement, unsupported add-on/OS, source not in role policy, or last-good-sync age above policy.

Do not make the primary search return malformed rows as drift: an unknown unit is not a safe numeric alarm. Conversely, do not let malformed/stale rows disappear from the dashboard. Source health must page the Splunk/Windows owner and cannot be suppressed by a time-maintenance exception.

Detect duplicate scripted input deployment by host, `_time`, raw hash, and input metadata. Repair duplicate app assignments. The primary `dedup` keeps the newest sample for evaluation but raw duplicates remain evidence; duplicate collection must not be treated as independent persistence.

Measure p99 indexing delay and align the 15-minute lookback with five-minute cadence. If endpoints can queue longer during network outages, source health reports delay and backfill; do not silently widen until a day-old sample becomes “current.”

## Step 5 — Create and understand the primary SPL

Save the sidecar SPL as `windows_time_offset_or_sync_error`. The base term fixes local index, vendor source type, and a 15-minute window. `eval` trims an ending `s`, parses numeric signed phase, takes absolute seconds for thresholding, parses the leading decimal error code, and selects `dest` before host for sample identity. `where` allows only complete, parseable records.

A deterministic descending sort by host, event time, and index time precedes `dedup`, so one newest valid sample per host remains. The threshold then returns absolute offset strictly above 120 seconds or nonzero error. `reason` distinguishes offset, error, or both. The output retains raw and normalized values. Event count is irrelevant, and the rule does not aggregate offsets across hosts.

Schedule every five minutes and trigger when result count exceeds zero. Use stateful incident handling keyed by stable host and reason. Close only after three consecutive fresh valid samples at or below a locally selected recovery threshold (for example 30 seconds) with error code zero and an approved source; missing/malformed data cannot recover. The 30-second/three-sample example is also local policy and must be tested.

Although Splunk lists the source type under Performance, validate tags/fields before any data-model use. A `tstats avg` can hide a latest 121-second sample behind older values and cannot represent raw error or unit confidence. Keep raw status primary.

## Step 6 — Validate thresholds and runtime behavior

Run the exact control tests with fixed times. Add offset values 119.999, 120.000, 120.001, negative equivalents, zero, very large finite values, malformed suffix, null, comma decimal, and code strings 0/5/nondecimal. Add two hosts, repeated host samples, event-time ties with distinct index time, stale sample, future sample, duplicate input, and newest recovery after older breach. Assert one row per host, absolute conversion once, strict boundary, correct reason, retained raw fields, and no lexical comparison.

On nonproduction Windows systems, compare every Splunk field with same-time `w32tm` commands. Create an offset only in an isolated lab using a supported test plan; never set a production clock backward/forward to test alerting. Safer fixtures can validate thresholds while normal command parity validates collection. Test loss of source/service under lab change control, restore, and confirm status/error and three-sample recovery.

Validate the effective Kerberos policy separately; do not assume five minutes if changed. Test application-specific effects only with owners. Record alert latency, search runtime, script duration, host CPU, status volume, scheduler concurrency, and deployment bundle behavior at fleet scale.

## Step 7 — Respond without unsafe clock changes

Alert text should state `Windows time status breach on <host>: offset=<seconds>, last_error=<code>, source=<source>`. Include UTC sample/index time, raw phase/error, stratum/reference, last good sync/time age, poll interval, role/domain/site/PDC, expected source, configuration revision, virtualization context, source health, threshold, exception, and runbook.

Responder sequence:
1. Verify newest raw status sample, field/unit parity, host identity, freshness, input/source health, and duplicate status.
2. Run the read-only `w32tm /query` commands and record same-time output/exit status.
3. Compare role and effective GPO/runtime configuration with expected domain hierarchy/manual source; identify forest-root PDC and recent role/config changes.
4. Check System events from `Microsoft-Windows-Time-Service`, including 129 domain-peer discovery and 134 manual-peer DNS failures, plus 35/37 synchronization context and 142 advertising state where relevant; read exact messages rather than relabeling IDs as offset.
5. Validate W32Time service/provider, DNS, NTP peer, UDP 123 path, network latency/asymmetry, firewall, host/hypervisor clock provider, power/resume/migration, and upstream authority health.
6. Assess Kerberos, certificates/tokens, logs, databases, clusters, backups, and applications against their actual tolerance before correction.
7. Apply only the approved Windows/AD/virtualization time runbook, then verify source, status, offset trend, error zero, role hierarchy, application health, and recovery samples.

Never automatically run `/resync`, unregister/register W32Time, change `NtpServer`, `Type`, `AnnounceFlags`, correction limits, Group Policy, hypervisor integration, system clock, PDC role, firewall, or service startup from the alert. A large correction or wrong source can disrupt authentication and event chronology.

## Step 8 — Exceptions, dashboard, and maintenance

Use only `lookup windows_time_status_exceptions.csv` as described in `knownFalsePositives`, after base detection. Include an approved maximum offset so an exercise expecting 130 seconds cannot hide 900 seconds. Preserve raw sample, exception revision, delivery decision, and recovery. Never suppress source health.

Build the dashboard exactly as described. Signed trend shows direction; absolute trend shows threshold. Display role-specific source compliance and last-good-sync age, not just offset. Keep current incident state separate from historical samples. Label every threshold/unit and timezone.

Troubleshooting:
- **No status sample:** inspect input enablement, app assignment, W32Time service/query output, script execution, forwarder queues, index/RBAC, and source health.
- **Phase parses null:** compare raw field and installed transforms with `w32tm`; fix version/locale extraction, never default zero.
- **Offset has wrong magnitude:** prove seconds versus milliseconds against same-time command before changing SPL.
- **Last error remains nonzero after sync:** verify current add-on output semantics, last successful sync, status refresh cadence, and later samples.
- **Source is Local CMOS Clock or VM provider unexpectedly:** verify hierarchy, PDC/virtualization policy, and recent changes; do not assume maliciousness.
- **Event time itself is wrong:** use `_indextime`, collector metadata, and external comparison to investigate; do not rewrite raw `_time` silently.
- **CIM differs:** inspect tags/aliases/acceleration and retain raw status authority.

Review host/role inventory, effective hierarchy, W32Time/add-on versions, input cadence, fields/units, parser tests, threshold/recovery, source health, lookup, dashboard, routing, retention, and runbook quarterly and after PDC, GPO, NTP, DNS/network, virtualization, Windows, add-on, or Splunk changes. Keep `status=draft` until Windows Time/AD and Splunk owners execute and sign all tests.
grandmaExplanation: We check the Windows clock's latest report and warn when it is more than two minutes away from its time source or when the last attempt to synchronize failed. Reliable clocks keep sign-ins, records, and investigations in the right order.
